title: A ceramics shop's three card-processing statements checked against its contract and Visa's published rates, five overcharges credited, a markup raised back to the first of the month, a regulated debit billed as exempt, a closed merchant ID, a wrong rate and a fee the contract does not name, while downgrades billed at their own rate, pass-through assessments, the fees the contract names, a credit already paid and a statement past its window are left alone
promise: A small online shop's processor statements for July, August and September are read line by line against the processing agreement, the processor's notices and Visa's published interchange schedule of 18 April 2026. Five overcharges are claimed for the amount they exceed: interchange billed at the wrong card product's rate, a regulated debit card billed at the exempt rate instead of the Regulation II ceiling, a markup raised by a notice that cannot reach back, a gateway fee for a merchant ID closed in 2025, and a PCI fee the agreement does not name. Downgrades billed at their own category's rate, assessments passed through at cost, the fees the contract names, a fee change made with proper notice, a chargeback fee already credited and a July line past its sixty days are left alone.
persona: The owner of a small online ceramics shop in Oregon, who takes Visa payments through a processor on an interchange-plus agreement and has never checked a statement
chore: Read the processor's statements, notices and guide, the processing agreement and the bank's debits and credits. Then compare each line with the agreement and with Visa's USA Interchange Reimbursement Fees of 18 April 2026 (and, for regulated debit, the Federal Reserve's Regulation II ceiling, 12 CFR 235.3 and 235.4) as they stand on 9 October 2026, and ask for a credit on each overcharge, inside the processor's sixty days.
command: I'm Nora, Wrenfield Ceramics. Check our Paycurrent statements for July to September against our agreement in Binderwell and the Ledgerwren bank, and ask Paycurrent to credit every line that was billed more than it should have been, and nothing else.

apps.name: Paycurrent
apps.role: the monthly statements and their lines, the processor's notices of price changes, its guide to the networks' fee schedules, and the form to ask for a credit

apps.name: Binderwell
apps.role: the processing agreement, clause by clause

apps.name: Ledgerwren bank
apps.role: what the processor debited, deposited and credited back

steps: Reads every statement line, the notices and the guide in Paycurrent.
Reads every clause of the agreement in Binderwell.
Reads the processor's debits and credits in Ledgerwren.
Back in Paycurrent, asks for a credit on the five lines that were overbilled.

gates.label: Ask the processor for a credit
gates.why: A claim to the processor, in the owner's name, that a line was billed against the agreement; a wrong one is an assertion the owner signed.

traps: Claiming a downgrade billed at its category's published rate.
Claiming interchange billed at the published rate of its card product.
Claiming assessments passed through at cost.
Claiming a fee the agreement names, or one added with the notice it requires.
Treating the exempt-issuer debit rate as an overcharge.
Claiming an overcharge the processor already credited.
Claiming a line from a statement past its sixty days.
memory: The rates Visa publishes for each category and card product, and the Regulation II ceiling, from Paycurrent's guide.
What the agreement allows: markup, fees, notice, merchant IDs and the sixty days, from Binderwell.
What the processor already debited and credited, from Ledgerwren, carried back to the last Paycurrent tab.

economics.basis: An estimate. A small shop on an interchange-plus agreement that nobody audits carries a few hundred dollars a month in fees the agreement does not allow, rates above the networks' published ones, and price changes made without the notice the contract requires; the roster's $4,000 a year is a small shop's share of those, recovered by asking for credits. The bench world holds $118: five lines on three statements (9.00, 34.20, 29.85, 15.00 and 29.95). Times a year: twelve, a monthly statement review. manual_minutes 120: reading three statements, the agreement and the notices, finding each card category's published rate, recomputing the lines, checking the bank for credits already paid and writing five requests. Rules applied, as they stand on Friday 9 October 2026: Visa USA Interchange Reimbursement Fees, Visa Supplemental Requirements, rates effective 18 April 2026 (consumer credit and debit, Card Not Present: Product 1, Non-Qualified, CPS/e-Commerce Basic and regulated debit); the Federal Reserve's Regulation II, 12 CFR 235.3(b) (21 cents plus 5 basis points) and 235.4(a) (a 1 cent fraud-prevention adjustment), whose 2023 proposal to lower the ceiling is not adopted and not used. Mastercard's own schedule (the April 2026 edition) could not be read, so no Mastercard line is in the world. The networks do not publish assessments in their interchange schedules: the world's 0.14% and 0.13% are the invented processor's pass-through schedule, at the level published processor schedules show. What moves a sale into Non-Qualified is the invented processor's own statement note, not a Visa text the world rests on.
economics.incumbent: Statement-audit services exist, but their published prices were not found for a figure that can be cited, so no incumbent_fee_pct is given.

sources.label: Visa USA Interchange Reimbursement Fees, Visa Supplemental Requirements, rates effective 18 April 2026 (consumer credit and debit, Card Not Present)
12 CFR 235.3(b), maximum permissible interchange fee for an electronic debit transaction (21 cents plus 5 basis points of the value)
12 CFR 235.4(a), fraud-prevention adjustment (1 cent a transaction)

edge.difficulty_why: Each line has to be set against a different published rate: a downgrade at the Non-Qualified rate is correct, the same card product billed at its neighbour's rate is not, a regulated debit has a ceiling that exempt debit does not, and a markup change is lawful only from the 30th day after its notice. The bank holds a credit that the statement does not, and one statement is past its window.
edge.usefulness_why: Recovers a few hundred dollars a year of fees the agreement does not allow, and does it in minutes rather than an afternoon with a rate table; a monthly chore, but the amounts are small, and most shops would not look.

expectation.why: A careful merchant with the agreement, the rate table and the bank in hand finds most of the five overcharges and claims none of the lookalikes, each for its exact amount, inside an hour.

caveat: Nora Whitlock, Wrenfield Ceramics, every statement, line, sale and amount, the Paycurrent Merchant Agreement and its clauses, the merchant IDs W-4471 and W-9020, the notices, and Paycurrent, Binderwell and Ledgerwren are invented; the processor's markup, its pass-through assessments at 0.14% and 0.13%, its settlement and address-verification conditions for its best category, its 60-day rule and its fees are the invented processor's own. The public rules applied are Visa's USA Interchange Reimbursement Fees of 18 April 2026 and the Federal Reserve's Regulation II as in force on 9 October 2026 (12 CFR 235.3(b) and 235.4(a)); Mastercard's edition could not be read, so no Mastercard rate is used, and Visa's qualification guide, which decides what makes a real sale downgrade, was not found public. A real processor's statement, a real contract and the issuer's actual category decide real cases. This applies stated rules to stated facts; it is not legal, tax or compliance advice.
